ENEL 585 – Dynamics & Control

Topic 11

Dr. Philippe Gray

Department of Electrical & Software Engineering

Dynamics & Control: The Plan

  1. Modelling: averaging over a switching period, perturbation and linearization, the small-signal model of the buck-boost converter
  2. Transfer functions: control-to-output and line-to-output, Bode plots, the right-half-plane zero
  3. Feedback: the loop gain, modelling the PWM, stability and phase margin
  4. Compensator design: PD, PI and PID compensators, and a full design example

Part 1: A Dynamic Model of the Converter

Why a Converter Needs Control

A real supply must hold \(v\) at its set value while \(v_{g}\) and the load \(R\) change

Feedback does this: measure \(v\), compare it with \(v_{ref}\), and let the error set \(d\)

The loop must:

Regulate Steady-state error within spec, ideally zero

Reject disturbances After a step in \(v_{g}\) or the load, \(v\) returns to \(v_{ref}\)

Stay stable \(v\) settles after any disturbance, over the full range of \(v_{g}\) and load

Be robust Despite component tolerances and effects the model leaves out

Respond well Rise time, overshoot and settling time within spec

Open Loop: Why a Fixed Duty Ratio Is Not Enough

A buck converter set for \(v=5\) V from \(v_{g}=12\) V at 1 A, with \(d\) held at \(D=0.425\):

The input drops \(V=D\,V_{g}\), so \(v\) falls with \(v_{g}\): 17 % low

The load rises 1 A to 4.6 A: more drop across the resistance of the switch and inductor

Start-up \(d\) at \(D\) from the first period: the \(L\)-\(C\) filter rings to 62 % above 5 V

Light load: DCM 0.15 A: \(i_{L}\) reaches zero each period and \(V\) is no longer \(D\,V_{g}\): 49 % high

The right \(d\) moves with \(v_{g}\) and the load, so it has to be set continuously from the measured \(v\)

What “Stable” Means

Same converter, three controllers: step the reference by a small \(\Delta v_{ref}\) and watch the output change, \(\Delta v\)

Stable \(\Delta v\) settles with no ringing

Stable, but ringing \(\Delta v\) settles after an oscillation that dies out

Unstable \(\Delta v\) never settles: here the oscillation grows until something limits it

Stable: after a small step, the output settles to a steady value.

Performance Targets

Three standard measurements describe how the output follows a step in the reference:

Rise time \(t_{r}\) The time \(\Delta v\) takes to go from 10 % to 90 % of \(\Delta v_{ref}\)

Overshoot How far the peak passes \(\Delta v_{ref}\), as a fraction of it: \(\;\dfrac{\Delta v_{peak}-\Delta v_{ref}}{\Delta v_{ref}}\times 100\,\%\)

Settling time \(t_{s}\) The time from the step until \(\Delta v\) stays inside a band around \(\Delta v_{ref}\), e.g. \(\pm 2\,\%\) of \(\Delta v_{ref}\)

Rejecting a Disturbance

Now hold the reference and step the load current \(i_{load}\) (or \(v_{g}\)): the output change \(\Delta v\) should return to zero

Peak deviation The furthest \(v\) is pushed from its value before the step

Recovery time \(t_{rec}\) The time from the step until \(\Delta v\) is back inside a chosen band around zero, and stays there

Full rejection \(\Delta v\) returns exactly to zero: the load changed, the output did not

Why We Need a Dynamic Model

For an ideal converter, steady state (\(V=M(D)\,V_{g}\)) says where \(v\) ends up, not how it gets there:

Inverting buck-boost: \(V_{g}=30\) V, \(R=10\ \Omega\), \(L=160\ \mu\)H, \(C=160\ \mu\)F

What steady state leaves out \(L\) and \(C\) store energy, so \(v\) cannot follow \(d\) at once: here it rings for milliseconds

A dynamic model Equations for how \(v\) responds over time to \(d\) and \(v_{g}\)

What it is for Deciding whether a loop is stable, and designing \(G_{c}(s)\)

What kind Holds for small changes around a steady state: a small-signal model

Two Time Scales: Ripple and Slow Variation

The same converter, with \(d\) now varied slowly: \(d(t)=0.60+0.02\,\sin(2\pi f_{m}t)\), \(f_{m}=50\) Hz

Two things at once \(v\) swings slowly between \(-49.0\) V and \(-41.4\) V at 50 Hz, with \(0.34\) V (peak to peak) of switching ripple at 50 kHz on top

What the dynamic model will describe Only the slow part: the average of \(v\) over one switching period (red). The ripple is left out

When averaging is valid When \(d\) varies much more slowly than the switching, so little changes within one switching period: here 50 Hz against 50 kHz

Steady State Plus a Small Change

Leave the ripple out and split each signal in two: \(\ v(t)=V+\hat{v}(t),\quad d(t)=D+\hat{d}(t)\)

Example: inverting buck-boost, \(V_{g}=30\) V, \(D=0.60\), \(\ V=-\dfrac{D}{1-D}\,V_{g}\)
Quotient rule: \(\dfrac{dV}{dD}=-\dfrac{(1-D)+D}{(1-D)^{2}}\,V_{g}=-\dfrac{V_{g}}{(1-D)^{2}}=-\dfrac{30\ \text{V}}{0.4^{2}}=-187.5\) V
\(\hat{d}=0.02\) gives \(\ \hat{v}\approx\dfrac{dV}{dD}\,\hat{d}=-187.5\times 0.02=-3.75\) V

The dc part and the ac part \(V\), \(D\): the steady state, the operating point
\(\hat{v}\), \(\hat{d}\): small variations around it: \(|\hat{v}| \ll |V|\), \(|\hat{d}| \ll D\)

Why small Near the operating point, the curve is close to its tangent, the line with the curve’s slope there, \(dV/dD\)

The steady-state prediction For low-frequency \(\hat{d}\), the converter is close to steady state at every instant, so \(\ \hat{v}\approx(dV/dD)\,\hat{d}\)
A dc result: at higher frequency, magnitude and phase differ (next slide; how low: Part 2)

Faster Variations: Magnitude and Phase Both Change

The same experiment, faster, with \(\hat{d}\) smaller so that \(\hat{v}\) stays small: \(\ \hat{d}(t)=0.005\,\sin(2\pi f_{m}t)\)

At 50 Hz \(\hat{v}\) matches the steady-state prediction: 2 % larger, and nearly in phase (lags by 3°)

At 400 Hz \(\hat{v}\) is 4 times the prediction and lags it by about 100°: this converter rang at 400 Hz after the step

At 1 kHz \(\hat{v}\) is a fifth of the prediction, and lags it by about 200°: more than half a period

Example converter: \(V_{g}=30\) V, \(R=10\ \Omega\), \(L=160\ \mu\)H, \(C=160\ \mu\)F, \(D=0.60\)

What the model must give The magnitude and phase of \(\hat{v}\) at every frequency: Part 2

Buck-Boost in CCM: Two Operating States

To develop the dynamic model, start as in steady-state analysis: the two states, with the duty ratio \(d(t)\) in place of \(D\), since it may now change from one period to the next

The converter

① \(0 \le t < dT_{s}\): \(Q_{1}\) on, \(D_{1}\) off

\(v_{L}(t)=L\dfrac{di_{L}}{dt}=v_{g}(t)\)
\(i_{C}(t)=C\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-\dfrac{v(t)}{R}\)

② \(dT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): \(Q_{1}\) off, \(D_{1}\) on

\(v_{L}(t)=L\dfrac{di_{L}}{dt}=v(t)\)
\(i_{C}(t)=C\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-i_{L}(t)-\dfrac{v(t)}{R}\)

Small Ripple, But No Longer Constant

Next, the small-ripple approximation. In steady state it replaced \(v_{g}\), \(v\) and \(i_{L}\) by their dc values:

\(\displaystyle v_{g}\approx V_{g},\qquad v\approx V,\qquad i_{L}\approx I_{L}\)

Now they vary, slowly. Replace each by its average over one switching period:

\(\displaystyle v_{g}\approx\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}},\quad v\approx\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}},\quad i_{L}\approx\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}\)

\(\displaystyle \langle x(t)\rangle_{T_{s}}=\frac{1}{T_{s}}\int_{t-T_{s}/2}^{\,t+T_{s}/2}x(\tau)\,d\tau\)

① \(Q_{1}\) on: \(\quad\displaystyle v_{L}\approx\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}},\quad i_{C}\approx-\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R}\)

② \(Q_{1}\) off: \(\quad\displaystyle v_{L}\approx\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}},\quad i_{C}\approx-\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}-\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R}\)

\(v_{g}\), \(v\) and \(i_{L}\) are nearly the same in ① and ②; \(v_{L}\) and \(i_{C}\) are not: each is averaged over both (next two slides)

Averaging the Inductor Voltage

\(d\): the fraction of this period with \(Q_{1}\) on, \(d'=1-d\); both can change from one period to the next

Average \(v_{L}\) over one switching period: the two shaded areas, divided by \(T_{s}\)

\(\displaystyle \langle v_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\Big[d\,T_{s}\,\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}} + d'T_{s}\,\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}\Big] = d\,\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}} + d'\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}\)

\(v_{L}=L\,\dfrac{di_{L}}{dt}\); average both sides:

\(\displaystyle \boxed{\,L\frac{d\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}}{dt} = d\,\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}} + d'\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}\,}\)

Volt-second balance, \(\langle v_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}=0\), is the steady-state case of this result

Averaging the Capacitor Current

\(d'=1-d\); both vary with time

Average \(i_{C}\) over one switching period, in the same way:

\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned}\langle i_{C}\rangle_{T_{s}} &= d\left(-\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R}\right) + d'\left(-\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}-\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R}\right)\\ &= -\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R} - d'\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}\end{aligned}\)

\(i_{C}=C\,\dfrac{dv}{dt}\); average both sides:

\(\displaystyle \boxed{\,C\frac{d\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{dt} = -\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R} - d'\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}\,}\)

Charge balance, \(\langle i_{C}\rangle_{T_{s}}=0\), is the steady-state case of this result

The Averaged Model Is Nonlinear

Together, the last two slides give the switching-period averaged model of the converter (averaged model for short):

\[ \begin{aligned} L\frac{d\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}}{dt} &= {\color{#c8102e}{d\,\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}}}} + {\color{#c8102e}{d'\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}}\\[4pt] C\frac{d\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{dt} &= -\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R} - {\color{#c8102e}{d'\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}}} \end{aligned} \]

Inputs: \(d\) and \(v_{g}\). Solving the two equations gives \(\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}\) and \(\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}\) as functions of time

Why it is nonlinear Each red term is a product of two signals that both vary with time

What that means A linear term is a constant times one signal, like \(\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}/R\): double the signal and the term doubles

A red term is a signal times a signal: double both and the term is four times as large

So the response does not scale with the size of the change

What we do about it Keep the changes small around the operating point and approximate each red term by a linear one, as was done for \(V(D)\) (next slides)

Part 2’s transfer functions need linear equations

Perturb Around the Operating Point

Write each averaged signal, and the duty ratio, as a dc value plus a small ac variation, the perturbation:

\[ \begin{array}{lrll} \text{input} & \langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}} &\kern-0.7em {}= V_{g}+\hat{v}_{g}(t) & |\hat{v}_{g}| \ll V_{g}\\[4pt] \text{input} & d(t) &\kern-0.7em {}= D+\hat{d}(t) & |\hat{d}| \ll D\\[4pt] \text{state} & \langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}} &\kern-0.7em {}= I_{L}+\hat{i}_{L}(t) & |\hat{i}_{L}| \ll I_{L}\\[4pt] \text{state} & \langle v\rangle_{T_{s}} &\kern-0.7em {}= V+\hat{v}(t) & |\hat{v}| \ll |V| \end{array} \]

\(d\) is already a per-period quantity: no ripple to average

Last column, the assumption: each perturbation is small compared with its own dc value

The operating point \(V_{g}\) and \(D\): the inputs, held constant
\(I_{L}\) and \(V\): the steady state that results, the averaged model with both derivatives set to zero

What the Split Does to a Product

The averaged model has three products of two signals. Take the first, and insert the split:

\[ \begin{aligned} d\,\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}} &= \big(D+\hat{d}\big)\big(V_{g}+\hat{v}_{g}\big)\\[4pt] &= DV_{g}+D\,\hat{v}_{g}+V_{g}\,\hat{d}+{\color{#c8102e}{\hat{d}\,\hat{v}_{g}}} \end{aligned} \]

The other two products contain \(d'\):

\(d'(t)=1-d(t)=D'-\hat{d}(t)\), with \(D'=1-D\)

\(DV_{g}\) A constant: the dc term

\(D\,\hat{v}_{g}+V_{g}\,\hat{d}\) Each is a constant times one perturbation: linear

\({\color{#c8102e}{\hat{d}\,\hat{v}_{g}}}\) A product of two perturbations: nonlinear, but a small quantity times a small quantity

With numbers \(D=0.6\), \(V_{g}=30\ \text{V}\), \(\hat{d}=0.01\), \(\hat{v}_{g}=0.5\ \text{V}\):
\(18\ \text{V}+0.3\ \text{V}+0.3\ \text{V}+{\color{#c8102e}{0.005\ \text{V}}}\)
60 times smaller than each linear term: neglect it

Inductor Equation: Perturb and Linearize

Insert the perturbations into the averaged inductor equation, \(\;L\,d\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}/dt = d\,\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}} + d'\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}\):

\(\displaystyle L\frac{d}{dt}\big(I_{L}+\hat{i}_{L}\big) = \big(D+\hat{d}\big)\big(V_{g}+\hat{v}_{g}\big) + \big(D'-\hat{d}\big)\big(V+\hat{v}\big)\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{L\frac{d}{dt}\big(I_{L}+\hat{i}_{L}\big)} = \underbrace{\big(DV_{g}+D'V\big)}_{\text{dc terms}} + \underbrace{\big(D\,\hat{v}_{g}+D'\hat{v}+(V_{g}-V)\,\hat{d}\big)}_{\text{first-order ac terms (linear)}} + {\color{#c8102e}{\underbrace{\hat{d}\,\big(\hat{v}_{g}-\hat{v}\big)}_{\text{second-order (nonlinear)}}}}\)

dc terms Right: \(DV_{g}+D'V=0\), volt-second balance, since the operating point is a steady state
Left: \(dI_{L}/dt=0\), since \(I_{L}\) is constant

Second-order term \(|\hat{d}\,(\hat{v}_{g}-\hat{v})| \ll |(V_{g}-V)\,\hat{d}|\)
since \(|\hat{v}_{g}| \ll V_{g}\) and \(|\hat{v}| \ll |V|\)
Neglect it: what is left is linear

What remains: the small-signal ac equation \(\displaystyle \boxed{\,L\frac{d\hat{i}_{L}}{dt} = D\,\hat{v}_{g}+D'\,\hat{v}+(V_{g}-V)\,\hat{d}\,}\)

Capacitor Equation: Perturb and Linearize

The same steps on the capacitor equation, \(\;C\,d\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}/dt = -\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}/R - d'\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}\):

\(\displaystyle C\frac{d}{dt}\big(V+\hat{v}\big) = -\frac{V+\hat{v}}{R} - \big(D'-\hat{d}\big)\big(I_{L}+\hat{i}_{L}\big)\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{C\frac{d}{dt}\big(V+\hat{v}\big)} = \underbrace{\Big(-\frac{V}{R}-D'I_{L}\Big)}_{\text{dc terms}} + \underbrace{\Big(-\frac{\hat{v}}{R}-D'\,\hat{i}_{L}+I_{L}\,\hat{d}\Big)}_{\text{first-order ac terms (linear)}} + {\color{#c8102e}{\underbrace{\hat{d}\,\hat{i}_{L}}_{\text{second-order (nonlinear)}}}}\)

dc terms Right: \(-V/R-D'I_{L}=0\), charge balance, since the operating point is a steady state
Left: \(dV/dt=0\), since \(V\) is constant

Second-order term \(|\hat{d}\,\hat{i}_{L}| \ll |I_{L}\,\hat{d}|\) since \(|\hat{i}_{L}| \ll I_{L}\)
Neglect it: what is left is linear

What remains: the small-signal ac equation \(\displaystyle \boxed{\,C\frac{d\hat{v}}{dt} = -\frac{\hat{v}}{R}-D'\,\hat{i}_{L}+I_{L}\,\hat{d}\,}\)

The Small-Signal Model

The last two boxed equations: the small-signal model

\[ \begin{aligned} L\frac{d\hat{i}_{L}}{dt} &= D\,\hat{v}_{g}+D'\,\hat{v}+(V_{g}-V)\,\hat{d}\\[4pt] C\frac{d\hat{v}}{dt} &= -\frac{\hat{v}}{R}-D'\,\hat{i}_{L}+I_{L}\,\hat{d} \end{aligned} \]

In the example, \(V=-45\ \text{V}\) and \(I_{L}=11.25\ \text{A}\):

\[ \begin{aligned} L\frac{d\hat{i}_{L}}{dt} &= 0.6\,\hat{v}_{g}+0.4\,\hat{v}+75\ \text{V}\,\hat{d}\\[4pt] C\frac{d\hat{v}}{dt} &= -\frac{\hat{v}}{10\ \Omega}-0.4\,\hat{i}_{L}+11.25\ \text{A}\,\hat{d} \end{aligned} \]

Linear, with constant coefficients Each term is a constant times one perturbation. The constants are fixed by the operating point

Two inputs, two states Inputs: \(\hat{d}\) (the control) and \(\hat{v}_{g}\) (a disturbance). States: \(\hat{i}_{L}\) and \(\hat{v}\)

When it holds Perturbations much smaller than the dc values: their products were neglected
Variations much slower than the switching: the signals were taken as nearly constant over one period

Two Models to Check

The averaged model

\[ \begin{aligned} L\frac{d\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}}}{dt} &= d\,\langle v_{g}\rangle_{T_{s}} + d'\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}\\[4pt] C\frac{d\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{dt} &= -\frac{\langle v\rangle_{T_{s}}}{R} - d'\langle i_{L}\rangle_{T_{s}} \end{aligned} \]

Leaves out the ripple: holds for variations slow against the switching. Nonlinear: \(d\) multiplies the signals

The linearized (small-signal) model

\[ \begin{aligned} L\frac{d\hat{i}_{L}}{dt} &= D\,\hat{v}_{g}+D'\,\hat{v}+(V_{g}-V)\,\hat{d}\\[4pt] C\frac{d\hat{v}}{dt} &= -\frac{\hat{v}}{R}-D'\,\hat{i}_{L}+I_{L}\,\hat{d} \end{aligned} \]

Also assumes small changes around the operating point \(D=0.6\). Linear. Plotted as \(V+\hat{v}\)

Next: both against the simulated converter, no averaging, after a step in \(d\)

How Good Is the Model?

A step in \(d\): simulated converter, no averaging averaged model linearized model

Small step, \(d\): 0.60 → 0.61. The linearized model stays within 0.2 V of the averaged model

Too large on purpose, \(d\): 0.60 → 0.75. Linearized around \(D=0.6\), it keeps the coefficients of \(D=0.6\): it ends at \(-45-187.5\times 0.15=-73\) V, not \(-90\) V, and rings at 400 Hz, not 250 Hz

In both plots the averaged model follows the converter: averaging loses only the ripple

One Linear Model per Operating Point

The linearized model holds near one operating point, but the converter works at many: if \(V_{g}\) falls from 30 V to 15 V with \(v\) held at \(-45\) V, \(D\) moves from 0.6 to 0.75

1. Linearize at each operating point Same equations, new coefficients: at \(D=0.75\), \(D'=0.25\), \(V_{g}-V=60\) V, \(I_{L}=18\) A. One set of transfer functions per operating point (Part 2)

2. Design one controller for all of them A single compensator that works at every operating point (Parts 3 and 4). Valid while the operating point moves slowly compared with the loop: a slow \(V_{g}\) drift, a soft-start ramp

3. Each model holds while \(\hat{d}\) stays small Every neglected term is \(\hat{d}\) times another change. A load step leaves \(D\) unchanged (\(V=-DV_{g}/(1-D)\)), so a well-designed loop moves \(d\) only briefly: load steps are what the loop is designed for

Fast, large moves of \(d\) A sudden large step in \(V_{g}\): a loop designed this way usually handles it. Solving the nonlinear averaged model with the controller gives the response to any one step, however large; a guarantee for every step needs large-signal analysis, beyond this course

Next: the transfer functions at one operating point, and their Bode plots

Part 2: Transfer Functions and Bode Plots

The Model in Matrix Form

Goal: transfer functions, \(\hat{v}(s)\) for a given \(\hat{v}_{g}(s)\) or \(\hat{d}(s)\): what Parts 3 and 4 design the controller with.
The two equations are coupled, so they are solved together. Divided by \(L\) and by \(C\) and stacked:

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\hat{i}_{L}\\[2pt] \hat{v}\end{bmatrix}}_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & \dfrac{D'}{L}\\[8pt] -\dfrac{D'}{C} & -\dfrac{1}{RC}\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{A}} \begin{bmatrix}\hat{i}_{L}\\[2pt] \hat{v}\end{bmatrix} +\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{D}{L} & \dfrac{V_{g}-V}{L}\\[8pt] 0 & \dfrac{I_{L}}{C}\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{B}} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\hat{v}_{g}\\[2pt] \hat{d}\end{bmatrix}}_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} \]

Laplace transform: \(d/dt\) becomes \(s\) Linear, constant coefficients, starts at the operating point (zero initial conditions): the differential equations become algebra
\(s\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s)=\mathbf{A}\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s)+\mathbf{B}\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)\), so
\(\displaystyle \boxed{\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s)=(s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{-1}\,\mathbf{B}\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)\,}\)

Four Transfer Functions

Write out the two vectors. \((s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{B}\) is a 2 by 2 matrix of transfer functions, one from each input to each state:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}\hat{i}_{L}(s)\\[4pt] \hat{v}(s)\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}G_{ig}(s) & G_{id}(s)\\[4pt] G_{vg}(s) & G_{vd}(s)\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\hat{v}_{g}(s)\\[4pt] \hat{d}(s)\end{bmatrix} \]

The second row is the output voltage, one term for each input:

\[ \hat{v}(s)=G_{vg}(s)\,\hat{v}_{g}(s)+G_{vd}(s)\,\hat{d}(s) \]

\(G_{vg}(s)\): line-to-output From the input voltage to the output voltage, with \(\hat{d}=0\): the disturbance the loop has to reject

\(G_{vd}(s)\): control-to-output From the duty ratio to the output voltage, with \(\hat{v}_{g}=0\): what the controller acts through

Solving for the Output Voltage

Inverted by hand; its determinant comes from \(\mathbf{A}\) alone: \(\;\Delta(s)=s^{2}+s/(RC)+D'^{2}/(LC)\):

\[ s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}s & -D'/L\\[3pt] D'/C & s+1/(RC)\end{bmatrix} \qquad\qquad (s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{-1}=\frac{1}{\Delta(s)}\begin{bmatrix}s+1/(RC) & D'/L\\[3pt] -D'/C & s\end{bmatrix} \]

The output voltage is the second row of \((s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{B}\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)\):

\[ \hat{v}(s)=\underbrace{\frac{-DD'/(LC)}{\Delta(s)}}_{G_{vg}(s)}\,\hat{v}_{g}(s) \;+\;\underbrace{\frac{(I_{L}/C)\,s-D'(V_{g}-V)/(LC)}{\Delta(s)}}_{G_{vd}(s)}\,\hat{d}(s) \]

\(G_{vg}\) in Standard Form

From the last slide:

\[ G_{vg}(s)=\frac{-DD'/(LC)}{s^{2}+s/(RC)+D'^{2}/(LC)} \]

Divide the top and the bottom by \(D'^{2}/(LC)\), so the constant term of the denominator is 1:

\[ G_{vg}(s)=G_{g0}\,\frac{1}{1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}} \]

Example
\(G_{g0}\) \(-D/D'\) \(-1.5\)
\(\omega_{0}\) \(D'/\sqrt{LC}\) \(2500\) rad/s: \(f_{0}=398\) Hz
\(Q\) \(D'R\sqrt{C/L}\) \(4\)

The dc gain is \(V/V_{g}\) At \(s=0\), \(G_{vg}=-D/D'=M(D)\)

The denominator is \(\Delta(s)\), from \(\mathbf{A}\) \(f_{0}\) is the 400 Hz ringing after the step

\(G_{vd}\) in Standard Form

From the slide before last:

\[ G_{vd}(s)=\frac{(I_{L}/C)\,s-D'(V_{g}-V)/(LC)}{s^{2}+s/(RC)+D'^{2}/(LC)} \]

Divide by \(D'^{2}/(LC)\) again, and use the steady state: \(\;V_{g}-V=V_{g}/D'\), \(\;I_{L}=DV_{g}/(D'^{2}R)\):

\[ G_{vd}(s)=G_{d0}\,\frac{1-s/\omega_{z}}{1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}} \]

Example
\(G_{d0}\) \(-V_{g}/D'^{2}\) \(-187.5\) V
\(\omega_{z}\) \(D'^{2}R/(DL)\) \(16\,667\) rad/s: \(f_{z}=2.65\) kHz
\(\omega_{0}\), \(Q\) as for \(G_{vg}\) \(f_{0}=398\) Hz, \(Q=4\)

The dc gain is the steady-state slope \(G_{d0}\) is the slope of the tangent, \(-6.25\,V_{g}\)

Only \(G_{vd}\) has a zero And it has a minus sign in it

\(G_{vd}\) at One Frequency: 400 Hz

For a sinusoidal \(\hat{d}\) at \(f=400\) Hz, put \(s=j2\pi f=j2513\) rad/s into the standard form:

\[ 1-s/\omega_{z}=1-j\,2513/16\,667=1-j0.151=1.011\angle{-8.6°} \]

\[ 1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}=1+j\,2513/10\,000-(2513/2500)^{2}=-0.0106+j0.2513=0.2516\angle 92.4° \]

\[ G_{vd}=-187.5\ \text{V}\times\frac{1.011\angle{-8.6°}}{0.2516\angle 92.4°}=-187.5\ \text{V}\times 4.02\angle{-101°}=-754\angle{-101°}\ \text{V} \]

Size: \(|G_{vd}|=754\) V \(\hat{d}\) of amplitude 0.005 gives \(\hat{v}\) of amplitude 3.8 V, 4.02 times the steady-state prediction

Phase: \(101°\) behind the steady-state prediction The prediction, \(-187.5\ \text{V}\times\hat{d}\), follows \(\hat{d}\) with no lag; \(\hat{v}\) lags it by \(101°\)

The minus sign: the converter inverts In the inverting buck-boost a larger \(D\) makes \(V\) more negative, so \(G_{d0}<0\), at dc too. The prediction has it as well, so it is not lag

Every frequency gives one point: repeat for each \(f\) and join the points, the curve on the next slide

\(G_{vd}\) Against Frequency

For a sinusoidal \(\hat{d}\) of frequency \(f\), set \(s=j2\pi f\): \(\;|G_{vd}|\) is the ratio of the two amplitudes, \(|\hat{v}|/|\hat{d}|\), and the angle of \(G_{vd}\) is the phase of \(\hat{v}\) against \(\hat{d}\)

The dot is the last slide At 400 Hz: 754 V, \(-101°\). The curve is the same calculation at every \(f\)

Phase: the lag, as on the last slide The minus sign of \(G_{d0}\) is left out. What it means for a feedback loop comes later in the course

Above 1 kHz \(|G_{vd}|\) is under 38 V: too small to read on these axes

Bode Plots

The next plots are the same transfer functions, with the same numbers, only on two different axes. A Bode plot is two plots against frequency on a logarithmic axis: the size of \(G(j2\pi f)\) in decibels, and its phase in degrees

\[ |G|_{\mathrm{dB}}=20\log_{10}|G| \qquad\qquad |G|=10^{\,|G|_{\mathrm{dB}}/20} \]

\(\lvert G\rvert\) 0.01 0.1 1 1.5 2 4 10
dB \(-40\) \(-20\) 0 3.5 6 12 20

If \(G\) is in volts, the result is in dBV, decibels against 1 V: \(187.5\) V is \(45.5\) dBV

Why a logarithmic frequency axis 10–100 Hz, 100 Hz–1 kHz and 1–10 kHz get the same width, so slow and fast variations are both visible. On the last slide the high frequencies were squeezed against zero

Why decibels \(|G_{vd}|\) goes from 764 V at the peak to 0.45 V at 25 kHz: invisible on a linear axis, but 57.7 and \(-6.9\) dBV both read easily

Products become sums In dB the factors of a standard form add, and so do their phases: the plot is the sum of theirs (next class)

\(G_{vg}\) as a Bode Plot

\(G_{vg}(s)=G_{g0}\,\dfrac{1}{1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}}\)
\(G_{g0}=-D/D'=-1.5\qquad\omega_{0}=D'/\sqrt{LC}\): \(f_{0}=398\) Hz\(\qquad Q=D'R\sqrt{C/L}=4\)

\(G_{g0}\): the level at low frequency \(|G_{g0}|=1.5\) is 3.5 dB. Phase without the minus sign of \(G_{g0}\), as for \(G_{vd}\)

\(f_{0}\): where it bends Above \(f_{0}\) the size falls by 40 dB for each factor of ten. The phase is \(-90°\) at \(f_{0}\)

\(Q\): the height of the peak At \(f_{0}\), \(|G_{vg}|=Q\,|G_{g0}|\): 4 times, 12 dB above the low-frequency level

One constant, one feature A larger \(R\) raises only the peak: \(Q\) has \(R\) in it, \(G_{g0}\) and \(f_{0}\) do not

\(G_{vd}\) as a Bode Plot: What the Zero Adds

\(G_{vd}(s)=G_{d0}\,\dfrac{1-s/\omega_{z}}{1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}}\qquad f_{0},\ Q\): as for \(G_{vg}\)
\(G_{d0}=-V_{g}/D'^{2}=-187.5\) V\(\qquad\omega_{z}=D'^{2}R/(DL)\): \(f_{z}=2.65\) kHz

Up to \(f_{0}\): as for \(G_{vg}\) Flat at \(|G_{d0}|=187.5\) V, 45.5 dBV, then the same peak, 12 dB higher at \(f_{0}\): the same denominator

Above \(f_{z}=2.65\) kHz the size falls more slowly The size of \(1-s/\omega_{z}\) grows by 20 dB for each factor of ten: well above \(f_{z}\) the size falls 20 dB for each, not 40

And the phase keeps falling A zero \(1+s/\omega_{z}\) would add \(+90°\); \(\;1-s/\omega_{z}\) adds \(-90°\). The phase passes \(-180°\) toward \(-270°\)

Next class Drawing these plots by hand from \(G_{g0}\), \(G_{d0}\), \(f_{0}\), \(Q\) and \(f_{z}\), and what the zero of \(G_{vd}\) does to a control loop

Drawing the Bode Plot by Hand

\[ G_{vd}(s)=\underbrace{G_{d0}}_{\text{constant}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\left(1-s/\omega_{z}\right)}_{\text{zero factor}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}}}_{\text{quadratic factor}} \]

Why by hand The computer gave the exact curve. A sketch from \(G_{d0}\), \(f_{0}\), \(Q\) and \(f_{z}\) shows which constant, and so which component, moves which part of it

Products become sums In dB the sizes of the three factors add, and so do their phases (“Bode Plots”): learn each factor’s plot once, then add

The pieces \(G_{vd}\) is a constant, a zero factor and a quadratic factor; \(G_{vg}\) is the same without the zero. The constant is a flat line; each factor gets a slide

First: one real pole (next slide) Not in \(G_{vd}\), but the simplest piece: well above \(f_{0}\) the quadratic factor falls like two of them, and the compensators of Part 4 use them

One Real Pole

\(G(s)=\dfrac{1}{1+s/\omega_{0}}\qquad f_{0}=\omega_{0}/2\pi\)
pole at \(s=-\omega_{0}\), where \(1+s/\omega_{0}=0\)

A pole An \(s\) where the denominator is zero: \(s=-\omega_{0}\). The plot’s \(s=j\omega\) never reaches it; its size \(\omega_{0}\) sets the bend, \(f_{0}\)

Below \(f_{0}\): nothing happens The factor is about 1: 0 dB and \(0°\). This straight line is an asymptote: the line the curve approaches

Above \(f_{0}\): \(-20\) dB per decade About \(\omega_{0}/s\), so \(|G|\approx f_{0}/f\): \(-20\) dB for each decade (factor of ten in \(f\)), and \(-90°\). The asymptotes meet at the corner, \(f_{0}\)

At \(f_{0}\): 3 dB below the asymptotes \(|1+j|=\sqrt{2}\): \(-3\) dB and \(-45°\). The phase asymptote runs from \(f_{0}/10\) to \(10f_{0}\)

A Real Zero, in Either Half-Plane

\(G(s)=1\pm s/\omega_{0}\qquad f_{0}=\omega_{0}/2\pi\)
A zero: a value of \(s\) where the numerator is zero. \(G_{vd}\) has \(1-s/\omega_{z}\): \(f_{z}=2.65\) kHz

\(1+s/\omega_{0}\): the pole upside down \(+20\) dB per decade above \(f_{0}\), and \(+3\) dB and \(+45°\) at \(f_{0}\)

\(1-s/\omega_{0}\) has the same size \(|1-j\omega/\omega_{0}|=|1+j\omega/\omega_{0}|\): a magnitude plot cannot tell the two apart

But its phase goes the other way From \(0°\) to \(-90°\): it lags like a pole, while the size rises

Left or right half-plane The factor is zero at \(s=-\omega_{0}\) (left half of the \(s\)-plane) or \(s=+\omega_{0}\): the right-half-plane (RHP) zero, \(G_{vd}\)’s. The plot’s \(s=j\omega\) passes neither

The Second-Order Denominator

\(G(s)=\dfrac{1}{1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}}\qquad f_{0}=\omega_{0}/2\pi\)
the denominator of \(G_{vg}\) and \(G_{vd}\): \(f_{0}=398\) Hz, \(Q=4\)

Below \(f_{0}\): nothing happens About 1: 0 dB and \(0°\), as for the pole

Above \(f_{0}\): \(-40\) dB per decade About \((\omega_{0}/s)^{2}\), so \(|G|\approx(f_{0}/f)^{2}\): \(-40\) dB for each decade, and \(-180°\)

At \(f_{0}\): the denominator is exactly \(j/Q\) So \(|G|=Q\) there: \(Q=4\) is \(+12\) dB, a peak. The phase is \(-90°\)

\(Q=0.5\): no peak \(-6\) dB at \(f_{0}\), the same as two equal poles, \((1+s/\omega_{0})^{2}\) in the denominator

Adding the Factors

\(G_{vd}(s)=G_{d0}\,\cdot\,(1-s/\omega_{z})\,\cdot\,\dfrac{1}{1+s/(Q\,\omega_{0})+(s/\omega_{0})^{2}}\)
\(|G_{d0}|=187.5\) V\(\quad f_{0}=398\) Hz\(\quad Q=4\quad f_{z}=2.65\) kHz

Sizes in dB add, and so do the phases \(|G_{d0}|\), plus the size of the zero, plus the size of the quadratic factor (\(1\) over the second-order denominator): as the “Bode Plots” slide promised

\(G_{d0}\): flat at 45.5 dBV The same at every frequency, and no phase of its own

The quadratic factor: 0 dB, then \(-40\) dB per decade From 398 Hz. Its straight-line phase falls \(180°\) between 298 and 531 Hz

The zero: 0 dB, then \(+20\) dB per decade From 2.65 kHz. Its phase goes from \(0°\) to \(-90°\) between 265 Hz and 26.5 kHz

The Asymptotes of \(G_{vd}\)

\(|G_{d0}|=45.5\) dBV\(\quad f_{0}=398\) Hz\(\quad f_{z}=2.65\) kHz\(\quad f_{z}/f_{0}=6.67\)

Up to \(f_{0}\): 45.5 dBV Flat at \(|G_{d0}|\). The exact curve is 57.6 dBV at \(f_{0}\): about \(Q\), 12 dB, above the asymptote

\(f_{0}\) to \(f_{z}\): \(-40\) dB per decade \(f_{z}/f_{0}=6.67\) is 0.82 decade: a 33.0 dB fall, so 12.5 dBV at \(f_{z}\). The exact curve is 15.7 dBV: about 3 dB above

Above \(f_{z}\): \(-20\) dB per decade The zero adds 20 dB per decade to the 40 that fall. At 25 kHz: \(-7.0\) dBV; the exact curve: \(-6.9\)

The phase \(0°\) up to 265 Hz, \(-193.5°\) at 531 Hz, then \(-45°\) per decade toward \(-270°\) at 26.5 kHz

The RHP Zero: The Wrong Way First

\(\langle i_{D}\rangle=(1-d)\,i_{L}\)
\(d\) steps from 0.60 to 0.62 at \(t=0\): the averaged model

The diode current is what feeds the output It conducts only while the switch is off: \(\langle i_{D}\rangle=(1-d)\,i_{L}\), and \(i_{L}\) cannot jump

At the step it drops, from 4.50 to 4.28 A The capacitor makes up the difference: \(v\) rises 43 mV toward zero in 61 µs. The wrong way

Then \(i_{L}\) builds up \(\langle i_{D}\rangle\) passes 4.50 A at 63 µs, and \(v\) heads for the new steady state, \(-48.9\) V

A right-half-plane zero does this More duty ratio first gives less output: the time-domain face of \(1-s/\omega_{z}\)

What the RHP Zero Means for Control

\[ f_{z}=\frac{D'^{2}R}{2\pi D L} \]

operating point \(f_{z}\)
\(D=0.6\), \(R=10\ \Omega\) 2.65 kHz
\(D=0.6\), \(R=5\ \Omega\) 1.33 kHz
\(D=0.75\), \(R=10\ \Omega\) 829 Hz

A fast controller pushes the wrong way One that reacted within about 120 µs would see \(v\) go the wrong way after raising \(d\), and raise \(d\) further

Above \(f_{z}\) the size still falls, but slowly \(-20\) dB per decade instead of \(-40\), while \(90°\) more lag comes in. A zero in the left half-plane would bring the phase back up

So act well below \(f_{z}\) The controller must be slow compared with the zero. Part 3 says how far below

\(f_{z}\) moves with the operating point Lowest at full load (smallest \(R\)) and the largest \(D\): that is the worst case
